The part of the rumour which is not true is that Mint's own ISO files were compromised. This may seem a small distinction, but it is important for a few reasons. The first is that existing links and torrents would continue to work as before. People downloading Mint from, for example, DistroWatch or Linux Tracker would be safe. Only people who stumbled across the bad link on Mint's site on the day it was visible would be affected. The second reason the link replacement is important is the attackers were unable to do anything about Mint's checksum or signature information. Anyone who checked the MD5 hash or publisher signature of the ISO file they downloaded would have immediately known they had the wrong ISO.

  • quidsup reading and reacting to the article above

"... Mint's website was hacked and their installation media replaced. This rumor is half true and perhaps all the more powerful for it." What? The rumor's not half true! It happened! It's a fact! A factual event that has happened is not a rumor.

  • The Linux Mint Blog » Blog Archive » Beware of hacked ISOs if you downloaded Linux Mint on February 20th!

Hackers made a modified Linux Mint ISO, with a backdoor in it, and managed to hack our website to point to it.

These three versions of events are not the same. I believe what actually happened was this: intruders created a poisoned ISO, then modified the download link on the Linux Mint website to point to their poisoned ISO. This means that only downloads from that link would be copies of the poisoned ISO. It also means that hash checks and signature verification against those provided by the Mint Team would fail, thus alerting downloaders to the fact that their ISO was not authentic. (The whole point of verifying digital signatures is to use public key cryptography to provide strong assurance that you're communicating with the party who owns the key associated with that signature.)

That is to say, there is no evidence that the official Mint image created by the Mint team was itself poisoned. That would be very bad, because it would leave the attackers in full control over the Mint team's own computers (that's the goal of a rootkit.) This would make it very difficult to prove that any future release of Mint was not also poisoned. This does not appear to be exactly what happened, at least not according to any reports I've read.

Please folks, check the hashes of your downloaded ISOs, and verify the digital signatures provided. This is the way you don't fall victim to poisoned ISOs. If the Linux Mint community had been acculturated to always do so, then very few if any would have been affected by the poisoned ISOs. "Trust" doesn't just mean you believe in the good intentions of your distro. It means that you, as a member of the user community, make the effort to responsibly verify that trust, and encourage others in your community to do the same.
